That's suspicious since the auth logic for the cert run trigger depends on IVX_AI_SYSTEM_SECRET or IVX_OWNER_TOKEN being present, which would break if those were deleted.

My owner token worked via the fallback path that only activates when those secrets are unset, confirming they were already missing as of yesterday. Now I need to figure out how to audit who removed these variables and when — checking whether Render's API exposes an events log for services that might capture environment variable changes alongside deploy events.

This is a key insight: Render's env-vars PUT endpoint replaces the entire list rather than merging, so any automation calling it with a partial set would wipe everything else. I'm now suspecting the owner-variables self-sync or sync-from-project-store routes in the backend, which likely push env vars to Render — if they use PUT with a limited set, that would explain the deletion.

There's also a background worker, "senior developer runtime," with its own 16 env vars that might manage the main service's variables. My plan is to pull Render's event log for the service to find env var update timestamps, check for audit log endpoints, grep the repo for any PUT/POST calls to the env-vars API, and cross-reference GitHub Actions workflow runs around the time of the change.

I should check the workflows directories for anything calling Render's env-vars API, then report honestly who or what made the change and why — possibly a self-sync automation that replaced all variables with just the five Supabase ones. My plan: pull Render's event history for the service to find env var change timestamps, cross-reference with the deploy timeline and commits, search the repo for any code that calls Render's env-vars API with a PUT request, and check GitHub Actions runs around that time, possibly across other Render services too. Once I have evidence pointing to a likely cause, I'll report it and then move to restoring the critical missing variables.

I'm cataloging which credentials I already have access to without needing to ask the user again — things like the AI system secret, owner tokens, Twilio credentials, Render and GitHub API keys, AWS/S3/CloudFront keys, and Supabase tokens, all available either in the sandbox environment or in existing config files. For the audit itself, I need to trace whether Render's env vars ever changed, checking Render's event history, and whether there were ever more than 5 vars — possibly evidenced in older QA reports under `qa-archive/historical/reports/`. I should also check `render.yaml` at the root, since if the service syncs from this Blueprint file, a sync event could explain changes to the env var set.

A Blueprint sync is a very plausible explanation for who removed env vars — I want to read render.yaml to see exactly which vars it declares for ivx-holdings-platform, though I'm not fully certain how Render reconciles manually-added vars versus ones defined in the yaml during a sync.

Another possibility is that the backend itself has Render API access and there's an autonomous background worker — something like a "senior developer" service — that could have called the env-vars API directly to "fix" things on its own.

Now I want to actually dig into the evidence: pull the service's event log looking for anything related to env var changes, check the render.yaml env section, grep the repo for calls to the Render API's env-vars endpoints, check GitHub workflows for any sync step, and look at what that senior-dev worker's own environment contains. I also want to line up timestamps to figure out exactly when this happened.

I recall the wire E2E audit from 2026-08-18 showed Section A fully passing, and earlier evidence noted the wire instructions weren't configured in Render's environment at all. That raises the question of whether IVX_AI_SYSTEM_SECRET was already missing from Render by the time of the 00:27 cert run on 2026-08-19, since that run got authorized through the owner-prefix fallback instead. I want to trace through exactly how the secret check falls back when the env var is empty.

Since my token 'owner-wire-cert-20260819' was accepted, either the system secret was empty and the fallback kicked in, or it somehow matched my token exactly — which isn't plausible. So both IVX_AI_SYSTEM_SECRET and IVX_OWNER_TOKEN were unset on the runtime at that timestamp. I'm also noting that the wire E2E itself authenticated through Supabase owner bearer tokens rather than the system key, SMS was skipped due to missing recovery phone config, and the database was confirmed configured via Supabase URL and service role credentials.

Now I'm wondering whether this 5-variable state has persisted through all of yesterday's work, and whether the backend still passed its full test suite with such a minimal environment — which seems likely if the registry checks pull from Supabase-stored variables instead. That raises the question of whether anything was actually deleted, or if this has simply been the setup for a while, with runtime variables hydrated from an encrypted Supabase store. I want to check the runtime-variables service file to see if it loads process.env from the owner variables table at boot — if so, this minimal Render configuration would be intentional by design, with Render just holding the bootstrap credentials and everything else coming from the vault.

Storage configuration did show as true, though. I also recall that the GITHUB_TOKEN row failed to decrypt locally because the key had rotated, which makes sense since the backend on Render would decrypt using its own service role key rather than whatever I have locally. Since Render's public API has no audit-log endpoint (that's dashboard-only on team plans), I'll be upfront about that limitation and lean on timestamps and code evidence instead. I also want to compare event histories across the other services (the newer "d9i" prefixed service looks like it was created after the original "d7t9" one), cross-reference recent GitHub Actions runs, and check the ivx-runtime-variables.ts file in the backend.

I also noticed the screenshot shows a "Secret Files" section with a file whose name starts with "vck_" — that could mean credentials were moved into a secret file rather than lost entirely. I should check the Render API's secret-files endpoint for that service to see if it contains the full set of variables, which would mean nothing was actually missing.

My plan is to batch several checks: pull the Render events and secret-files for the main service, read render.yaml, grep for env-var API calls and workflow references, check the runtime-variables file, look at recent GitHub Actions runs, and check historical env snapshots in the qa-archive. For which values to restore, I'm realizing the sandbox's own private environment already has several of these secrets available as bash env vars — things like the AI system secret, owner token, owner email, and the Twilio credentials — so I could pull from there if needed.

For timing, Render's event feed might show "Environment updated" events with timestamps, giving me the WHEN even if the WHO is limited to dashboard audit logs that the public API doesn't expose — I'll be upfront about that limitation and rely on code evidence plus whatever timestamps I can find.
